newsitem.title: UK: Most metals end LME higher, funds motor prices up.
newsitem.headline: Most metals end LME higher, funds motor prices up.

text.p: A late flurry of buying during Friday afternoon LME trading kept most base metals on the boil, with prices largely firmer at the close.

Traders said the complex seems to have shrugged off the mid-week wobble when a tumble in copper sent others into a tailspin. Today, copper continued to recover as nearby spreads moved out once more, while investment fund buying fostered strong advances in zinc and nickel.
"All told, it's been a good start to the year for prices. Most are higher, and the funds are probably looking to play it from the long side," one trader said.

Copper trading again featured spread activity, as the nearby prompts remained fully firm. Cash/one day was at $23 this afternoon, just under the LME limit, while cash/one week was $95 backwardation. Beyond the Feb dates, the market tightness is not so acute, with Feb/one week at $9. The overall cash/threes backwardation is at $225.

Because of the high nearby premium, stocks are being attracted to the market, which was why the 26,100-tonne increase in LME stocks was virtually ignored. Total inventories now stand at 191,750 tonnes -- the highest since October 1995.
A possible medium-term bear signal will be if these stocks stay high once the backwardation has passed as this would indicate that metal has not merely been lent to the market, traders said.

However, in the short-term, the market is expected to continue a strong technical bounce. After touching the year's low of $2,140 early today, three months sped higher, breaking $2,180 to end at $2,186, up $26 from Thursday.
Aluminium prices were steadier, with a 10,750-tonne drop in stocks providing some impetus, although the market consistently stalled at the $1,625 chart barrier.
"This was a pretty important level in the recent rise, so it's not a surprise there should be sellers there," another trader said.
Last trade was at $1,624, up $10 from the overnight kerb close.
Nickel reached its highest levels for 4-1/2 months, as the undercurrent of fund interest swelled movements in a market seeing signs of consumer buying, traders said.
The solid 894-tonne stock draw in Europe and the suddenness of the price advance may have convinced some end-users that levels below $7,000 were not going to be re-visited soon.
Last business was at $7,585, down from a $7,640 peak as there was some profit-taking around $7,600, although this was still up $290 from Thursday.

Zinc continued to trade around the dizzy heights reached this morning, with the expected profit-taking and consolidation likely to be short-lived. The strength of the rally of the last 24 hours -- with prices leaping from near $1,120 to two-year highs of $1,174 -- suggests there are further gains to come.

Traders said the physical market is likely to confirm this trend, with stocks seen falling consistently. Next week's industry meeting in the U.S., meanwhile, should also foster some positive sentiment. Last trade was at $1,169, up $33.

By contrast, the lead market was sluggish, and prices have yet to display a convincing rally from Thursday's lows. Prices closed $1 easier at $672. Tin made some headway, but trade was generally low-key. Final business was at $5,855, up just $35.
The alloy market was quietly steadier at $1,525/27 a tonne.
